Each Viewed entry offers Mark as unviewed, which drops that file's snapshot without touching the Git index, so its whole change from the branch base is listed under Changes again; unviewing a file that isn't a current Viewed entry, including one already unviewed and an unknown path, is rejected. These results persist across fresh CLI/XPC connections. The Changes section collapses inside the task sidebar, hiding its Viewed and Changes lists while its header and pending count stay visible and the sidebar stays open for other sections; separately, the whole sidebar hides to a narrow rail that still shows how many files are pending. Each collapsed or expanded state is its own global preference, so opening another task keeps it. Once loaded, refreshing a task with no changes keeps its No changes state on screen instead of flashing the loading placeholder.

A newly created task branch with no branch or worktree changes starts with empty Viewed and Changes sections. External Git commits unique to the task branch and staged, unstaged, or untracked edits update the open task's Changes sidebar automatically; commits unique to the base branch are excluded. Fresh CLI connections report the same per-file inventory. When the base branch's local copy is stale behind its origin remote-tracking branch and the task branch has merged the newer upstream commits, those commits are excluded as well, so the inventory matches the pull request instead of the stale local branch. A local base branch that is ahead of its remote-tracking branch stays the base, so unpushed base commits merged into the task branch are not listed as task changes. While a merge is still open in the task's worktree, its files are held back and the sidebar shows a 'Merge in progress' notice naming the repository instead of the files the merge staged; the CLI reports the repository under mergingRepositories with empty sections, and aborting the merge lists the task's changes again.

A task whose worktree holds more than 1000 changed files still reports every one of them through fresh CLI connections, while the open task's Changes sidebar shows a 'Too many changes to list' notice naming the count instead of rendering the file list, so the window stays responsive. Bringing the count back under the limit lists the files again.

Each task's sidebar ends in a command row whose buttons sit at its right edge; it holds a terminal button. The terminal only ever opens in the task's created repository worktree, never in its source repository or a context folder, and never creates a worktree itself: while the task's worktree is still pending, or the task has no repository, the button is disabled and the CLI reports terminal_unavailable without creating the worktree, and the button enables in the open conversation once the worktree is created. The CLI reports how the terminal starts: the account's executable login shell with -l in that worktree, with TERM=xterm-256color and PLAYHOUSE_TASK_ID set, and the same answer on a fresh CLI/XPC connection; running that shell in that folder prints the worktree path and the task ID. Clicking the button slides a terminal panel in from the window's right edge, floating over the conversation's right side without moving or resizing the conversation, whose shell runs in the task's worktree with the task ID in its environment and which uses macOS Terminal's Clear Dark ANSI palette (such as its blue, distinct from the emulator's own default) on a solid black background, switching to the Clear Light profile's white background and blue when the app's appearance turns light and back when it returns to dark; hiding the panel keeps the same shell, so reopening it reaches the same process. Dragging the panel's left border resizes it against the right edge, between a 320-point minimum and leaving 260 points of conversation uncovered, without resizing the conversation, and reopening the panel keeps the dragged width. Typing exit shows that the shell exited, and Restart starts a new shell, with a different process, in the same worktree. A task whose worktree no longer exists reports terminal_unavailable from the CLI, and the panel shows that error with a Try Again action that opens the shell once the worktree is back; an unknown task ID and the standalone chat's ID are not_found, and the standalone chat offers no terminal button.

The CLI confirms a new repository-backed task persists in Backlog; the UI shows no PR control there, then shows the active-card PR action after the conversation completes with a minimum 30-point hit target, on its own last row below the card title and time row and on the right, with that row absent while the task sits in Backlog. The active-card PR control visibly presents its native help on hover, while hovering the card itself shows no tooltip and the card remains an openable control; the Done archive PR action remains available with its completed-task label and visibly presents its native help on hover, then waits for the task lock before a real GitHub CLI or branch publication failure without saving a PR link or changing Done status. The card's PR button shows its full PR label with its hover capsule around it, not a truncated ellipsis; the JavaScript task item composes it the same way, as a borderless 30-point button whose 10-point capsule overhangs it, labelled PR.

A working-state task card (In Progress, Blocked, or Waiting Response) with no linked pull request shows a compact pull request mode pill in place of the manual PR button, closed on its current mode and defaulting to PR; clicking it slides out Manual, PR, Green, and Merge, and choosing one selects it and folds the pill back onto it. The pill stays beside linked pull requests so autopilot and merge remain switchable. Selecting PR persists as mode pr with Auto PR on and is reflected across a fresh read; `task pr mode` accepts manual, pr, autopilot, and merge (autopilot and merge also turn Auto PR on) and rejects an unknown mode without changing the task. When a turn completes while Auto PR is on, Playhouse creates the task's pull request itself on the way to Review with no user click, exactly once. When Auto PR stays off, the task still reaches Review with no pull request, and the existing manual PR button still creates it afterward unchanged. Every new task starts in PR mode, whatever mode the previous task was left in; changing one task's mode never changes the default for later tasks. Toggling Auto PR for an unknown task is rejected.

`task pr status` reports each linked PR's check state, failing check names, and a green, red, or pending health, and reads unresolved review threads only for an autopilot task; the board colours each linked PR number green, red, or blue by that health and keeps the mode pill beside linked PRs. Autopilot leaves a task inactive unless its mode is autopilot and it sits in Review. With checks still running it sends no turn, and the board re-probes only those autopilot PRs on a slow poll until they settle. When checks fail or review threads are unresolved it sends one visible Playhouse autopilot fix turn through the task's provider that names the failing checks and unresolved threads, asks the model to judge every comment critically and to reply to and resolve each thread whether or not it changes code, and allows waiting-response for blockers it cannot fix (such as a GitHub outage or a Jira ticket the user must add); the task is In Progress during that turn and returns to Review when it reports completed. Once the PR is green autopilot sends nothing, never merges it, and resets its loop guard, so the same red state returning later (picked up by the focus probe) is fixed again. A fix turn that reports waiting-response stops the loop until the user sends the task back to Review, after which autopilot may try the red PR once more; a red state unchanged since the last fix moves the task to Waiting Response with a reason instead of being sent again, and the CLI case also drives the five-attempt cap to its Waiting Response stop. A check rerun counts only by its latest run, as on GitHub: a failure followed by a newer success reads green with no failing checks, a success followed by a newer failure reads red naming the check, and same-named checks from different workflows stay separate (one failing workflow still reads red, failing names listed once), as do commit status contexts by context and untimed entries by rollup order.

Merge mode does everything autopilot does (it reads review threads, and red pull requests take the same autopilot fix path covered by the autopilot case) and also merges each linked pull request once it is green: with checks still running, or no checks reported yet on a freshly pushed head, it merges nothing and the task stays in Review; once checks pass (or the head has had no checks past the registration grace, as in a repository without CI) with no unresolved threads and GitHub reporting it mergeable, it merges the PR through GitHub CLI, pinned to the head commit it saw green, with the first merge method the repository allows (squash when allowed, otherwise a merge commit), exactly once; the PR reads as merged, the task stays in Review for the user to complete, and the card shows the merged completion action. A head that still has no checks after the registration grace is merged all the same. A merge GitHub refuses (for example a required review) moves the task to Waiting Response with GitHub's reason instead of retrying.

The real Git CLI detects merge conflicts without mutation, and PR creation still publishes the task branch and reaches the normal GitHub CLI path; conflicts do not block PR creation. CLI/XPC resolves staged conflicts locally without pushing and commits and pushes a staged resolution without changing the target. The paired UI confirms PR creation proceeds for a conflicted branch and the existing Fix Conflicts action still appears once the PR is linked.

Separate Review task cards probe their linked pull requests concurrently on app focus, with refreshes limited to one per 20 seconds, with focus events during cooldown coalesced into one trailing refresh. A conflicting PR or a mergeable PR whose remote head is not pushed locally retains the imported conflict action with its indicator artwork beside its PR link; the UI renders the artwork inside the action, keeps it beside the PR link, and gives both controls hit targets of at least 30×30 points. Clicking the conflict action sends the corrected request in the task conversation. CLI and UI use the same GitHub mergeability and head checks, retry once when resolution remains unconfirmed, and clear the action only after GitHub confirms the pushed head.

A completed turn outcome on a task with a PR-linked repository and a configured remote commits local work, merges new remote pull request commits, and pushes the branch before the task reaches Review, so the reviewed worktree holds no local-only changes. A linked repository without a publishing remote is left untouched and still reaches Review. When the sync cannot complete, the task moves to Blocked with the sync failure message instead of resting in Review, and a later successful sync pushes the stranded commits and returns the task to Review. While a provider turn holds the task's worktree, the sync command skips it untouched and reports turn-active. A worktree switched off its task branch fails the sync with a message naming both branches and blocks the task, leaving that other branch and the remote untouched; once switched back, a remote commit whose changes the branch already holds is concluded as a merge commit and pushed, the task returns to Review, and the next sync is up-to-date instead of failing on an unfinished merge. A merge Git refuses outright, such as one with unrelated history, blocks the task with Git's own error after the generic merge failure message, and restoring the remote branch heals it back to Review. A clean merge an earlier sync left unfinished on the task branch is concluded as a merge commit and pushed. A task branch deleted on a reachable remote is reported as no-remote-branch and leaves the task in Review.

When the remote pull request branch conflicts with local task commits, the review sync merges the remote branch and instructs the task's provider to resolve every conflict; if conflicts remain after the provider turn, the sync fails, the task moves to Blocked with the sync failure message, the merge stays in progress for manual resolution, and the remote branch is unchanged. A rerun with the conflicts staged commits the resolution, pushes the merged branch, and returns the task to Review. The board triggers the same sync automatically when a mergeable pull request's remote head diverges from the local head.

CLI/XPC creates PRs for two repositories, verifies the first PR persists when the second creation fails, retries only the missing repository, confirms each gh create call targets the corresponding repository worktree, and confirms both saved numbers on fresh reads. The UI labels active-card and Done-archive multi-repository creation actions PRs, clicks the active action, verifies the partial-success retry action, confirms the gh create calls target both repository worktrees and retry only the failed one, then shows exact PR numbers on the active task and Done archive, including four-digit values without grouping separators, each with a hit target at least 30 points wide and tall. Hovering the outer padded edge of each PR link triggers its feedback.

PR creation opens a pull request only for repositories whose task branch has commits its merge target lacks: in a two-repository task where only the primary worktree changed, gh create runs once, against the primary worktree, the primary saves its PR number on a fresh read, and the unchanged secondary keeps no PR link instead of failing the whole operation with GitHub's no-commits error and is remembered as skipped at its branch head, so the card offers no further create action; a review sync with no change keeps the skip, and once the primary's pull request merges and the task moves to Done, the Done archive shows the primary's PR link and no create action either. A two-repository task whose every repository is unchanged is rejected with a message saying no repository has changes to open a pull request for, with no gh create call and no PR link saved, and both repositories are remembered as skipped. After the task changes one of them, the review sync clears only that repository's skip, the card's create action counts it alone as a single PR, and creating it opens exactly one more pull request, for that repository. A later change to the still-skipped repository beside that linked PR brings back a single create action for the repository without a linked pull request, and creating it links that repository too. The UI shows the primary's PR link after clicking the PRs action and reports the all-unchanged message in the failure alert.

Explicit app overrides reject obsolete compatibility metadata, foreign worktree or bridge identities, test IDs that do not match the current worktree, and nonisolated test data before launching; the current app preserves a saved draft across restart.
An invalid legacy database fails import without changing the source or publishing a destination or partial snapshot; the normal isolated board remains usable.

New tasks use the default provider from settings, which starts as Codex and rejects unknown providers, and task create can choose a provider explicitly and saves a --prompt description without starting the task, rejecting a blank or missing prompt; the UI shows that task in Backlog with the description unsent in its composer. A task without a conversation switches providers immediately; provider choice persists across fresh CLI/XPC reads and an app relaunch. Each provider's selected model is global across conversations and persists across provider switches and fresh CLI/XPC reads without reusing the other provider's model. Unknown providers and Done-task switches are rejected, and history has no provider boundary. A Claude task names Claude in the empty conversation, hides Goal mode, and rejects Goal changes through CLI/XPC. Switching a task's provider also updates the sticky default provider for new tasks and chats.

After a completed Codex fixture turn, switching providers is rejected while a follow-up is queued or a turn is active, and the provider menu is disabled during the turn. A settled switch to Claude records a boundary after the last Codex reply that persists across fresh reads and an app relaunch, keeps the Codex thread, and keeps earlier replies labeled Codex; switching back before any Claude turn removes the empty boundary, and the next Codex turn completes in the same thread.

Against the Claude Code protocol fixture, the answer Claude writes before running its Playhouse progress and outcome commands and the closing line it adds afterward form one final answer, not commentary, in the streamed final answer, fresh history, and transcript, and the reported outcome moves the task to Review. Text Claude writes before an ordinary tool stays commentary, and a turn that leaves every status nudge unanswered ends in Blocked. The fixture records all five private nudge attempts for each unreported turn; fresh history shows the nudge prompts and their replies. Switching to Codex hands off the whole Claude answer, excludes answered-turn commentary and private nudge prompts and replies including their redacted placeholders, and hands off only the last commentary from the turn that recorded no answer. A new Claude conversation with no explicit model pick dispatches to Sonnet and shows Sonnet as the picker default.

A standalone chat reports no task outcome, so it ends every turn with Playhouse's own chat page close-turn signal. When Claude runs that signal after its answer and before its closing line, the answer and closing line form one final answer, not commentary, in the streamed final answer, fresh CLI/XPC history, and the visible transcript, so the response is never left buried inside the collapsed Worked for disclosure; text written before an ordinary tool earlier in the same turn still stays commentary there, and the close-turn command really runs and succeeds. The chat instructions ask for close-turn before the final reply, which must end the turn, keep exactly one real close-turn per turn and no page bookkeeping in the answer, and carry no hidden escalation. A turn that runs close-turn first and answers after it shows exactly one final answer, filed onto the active page, with no nudge. When the turn ends on close-turn and Claude Code adds its own no-visible-output notice to the same turn, the notice streams once as a user-side message and stays in fresh history between the answer and what Claude writes after it, rendering as an automatic message from Claude Code rather than the user's bubble; that later text is a separate final message, so no bubble holds the answer twice, and the notice is never filed into a chat page. This classification is Claude-specific because Playhouse derives each message's phase from Claude's tool stream and only Claude Code adds such a notice inside a turn, while Codex reports the phase in its own protocol and never injects a hidden message into a turn.

When a standalone chat turn ends without its chat page close-turn signal, Playhouse sends exactly one follow-up turn through the same unsettled-turn recovery loop task conversations use. Its prompt starts with the Playhouse nudge marker, asks for close-turn on the previous reply and never for a task outcome, and stays in the chat transcript as an automatic message from Playhouse, followed by the agent's reply. A close-turn run in that nudge settles the turn and classifies the user's turn, which moves to the new titled page without the fallback classifier; the nudge turn and its reply are never filed into a chat page or replayed into a page's seeded context. A nudge that goes unanswered is not retried, the background classifier then decides the page, the chat never gets a board status such as Blocked, and task outcome is rejected for the chat. The nudge loop, the close-turn CLI and the turn outcome store are shared by Claude and Codex, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case, and the round-trip case shows a Codex chat turn reaching the same nudge.

A standalone chat turn that is still running when its daemon dies is followed by the next daemon, and when it ends with close-turn --continues false that daemon files the turn's question and answers on the new titled page the close-turn opened, exactly once, leaving the earlier page as it was and no page decision pending. The page's first session is seeded with that turn, so the next question reaches the provider with the turn's question and answer. Filing reads Playhouse's own close-turn record and turn transcript, shared by Claude and Codex once a reattached turn ends, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

A standalone chat turn that ran close-turn --continues false and then lost both its daemon and its agent before it was filed is filed, question included, by the next daemon on the page that close-turn opened, found from Playhouse's durable close-turn record. An answered turn that an earlier build left unfiled after its close-turn opened a new page, with no close-turn record, is filed by the next daemon as it starts onto the page opened while that turn ran. Both recoveries are recorded in diagnostics, a further daemon restart files nothing again, and the next question's fresh page session is seeded with the recovered turn. Recovery reads only Playhouse's own transcript, close-turn record and page store, so provider selection cannot change it; one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

A Codex standalone chat turn survives daemon restarts even though Codex's own history carries no message times. A turn still running in its shared app-server when its daemon dies is followed by the next daemon, and when it ends with close-turn --continues false that daemon files its question and answers once on the new titled page, found from the turn's durable in-flight record and close-turn record, with no page decision left pending. A turn whose daemon and app-server both die after its close-turn opened a new page is filed on that page, with what its thread saved, by the next send, which reads the Codex thread before seeding; that send's fresh page session carries the recovered turn, and the recovery is recorded in diagnostics.

A standalone chat turn that is still running when its daemon dies and then ends without close-turn is filed by the daemon that followed it on the active page, marked as a missed page signal, and handed to the background page classifier, which moves it to the new page it titles; the earlier page keeps only its own turn and nothing stays pending. When the daemon instead dies during the close-turn nudge that follows a turn without close-turn, the daemon that follows the nudge files the user's turn, never the nudge, hands it to the classifier the same way, and the chat keeps accepting sends. The missed-signal and classifier path is shared by Claude and Codex once a reattached turn ends, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

The model picker removes the Default entry, superseded aliases, older versions, and duplicate snapshots, keeping only the newest concrete version in each family. GPT-6 Luna replaces GPT-5.6 Luna, and Claude Opus 5.5 replaces the Opus alias and older snapshots. Claude Code names its newest release only through an alias entry's resolved model, so that resolved version supersedes the older concrete Opus 5 and keeps Claude Code's own display name. Alias entries with no resolved model are omitted. A remembered selection the filtered list no longer offers moves to its family's newest offered model and is written back, surviving a later refresh whose list no longer offers that family, while a still-offered selection is left alone. A remembered bare alias migrates to its family's offered release, but a dated snapshot pinned through the CLI is left in place because its family's undated release is not a higher version. The shared CLI/XPC list applies the same filtering to Codex and Claude, and the visible picker matches the Codex list. The model popover opens above its composer control.

The selected effort persists through CLI/XPC reads and reaches Codex turn/start collaborationMode.settings.reasoningEffort; a model's advertised effort limit rejects unsupported requests before history is created. The UI selects Extra High and sends a Sol turn, then simulates a legacy transcript with no Codex turn metadata and sends a Luna turn; the old reply remains provider-only and the new reply is attributed to Luna. The latest reply shows its provider timestamp, while a legacy history item without createdAt has no timestamp label.

Right after a Codex turn on a non-default model (Sol) ends, loading history with Sol still selected reuses the loaded thread, and after the selection moves to another non-default model (Mini) it resumes with that selected model rather than the hardcoded default and succeeds even though Codex, still holding the thread open, reports Sol; the reply stays visible with no conversation error. A later send on Luna still confirms the model Codex reports and fails with a model mismatch instead of switching silently, without starting a turn, and the next Luna send whose model Codex confirms succeeds.

Claude's model picker omits Default and aliases, showing Opus 5.5 resolved from Claude Code's bare alias entry as the concrete latest choice in place of the older Opus 5. Selecting it changes the prompt and reply label to Claude · Opus 5.5, and later model changes preserve the old reply's model attribution. The selected effort persists through CLI/XPC reads and reaches Claude Code as CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL; the UI selects Extra High and sends a Claude fixture turn whose recorded environment value is xhigh.

Codex and Claude filtered model lists persist across fresh CLI/XPC requests; an unavailable workspace fails refresh without clearing the previous cache. The visible Claude picker shows the seeded cached option before replacing it with the filtered versioned provider list, and retains an offline cached option when the provider executable is unavailable.

A misplaced pending question can be repaired through CLI/XPC only into its owning conversation. Repair rejects a wrong owner and a conflicting destination without mutation, applies both tasks' state atomically, preserves request identity and mode, clears only the misplaced source, and is retryable. Fresh history and the visible UI restore the question only on the original task; answering it clears pending state and the safe response survives reopening. Retrying an interrupted repair after the destination question was answered rejects the stale source without resurrecting the question.

The bridge daemon starts on the first request, exactly once even when callers race to start it, serves later requests from the same process, and stays alive while any connection (such as a window's runtime or CPU usage watcher) is open. A watcher receives the daemon's runtime snapshots as a turn starts and stops, and the daemon exits by itself once the last connection closes and no request is running; the next request starts a fresh daemon on demand without any manual step.

When the bridge daemon dies in the middle of a turn, that turn's send fails with a connection error instead of hanging, but the provider keeps running in its own session. The next request starts a fresh daemon on demand, which reattaches the running turn so the task stays In Progress with no restart notice, stops that reattached turn, and can then run and stop a new turn.

A Claude Code turn that writes its result while no daemon is running is finished by the next daemon from the run's log: the task leaves In Progress through the normal outcome path without a restart notice, and the result written during the downtime appears exactly once.

On a daemon's first request for a data folder, a process whose standard streams point into the folder's Claude or Codex run directories but that no run or server manifest accounts for is stopped, while a process writing into a run or server whose spawn is still being recorded is left alone.

`conversation watch` (conversation.events.subscribe) on a task with no running turn returns at once with watched=false, and fails for an unknown task. While a turn another caller sent is running, a watcher receives a `watching` event, the turn's live text deltas and its final `completed` history, while the sender still gets its own stream; the window streams such a turn the same way.

Stop works on a turn a fresh daemon reattached: for Codex it sends turn/interrupt over the reconnected socket and leaves the shared server running; for Claude it sends the interrupt with a request number past the old daemon's and then kills the run by its verified process identity and removes its folder. Either way the task settles in Waiting Response without a restart notice.

When a Codex app-server or a Claude Code run exits without finishing its turn while no daemon is connected, the next daemon settles the task as Waiting Response with 'The agent stopped while Playhouse was restarting. Your conversation is saved; send a follow-up to continue.', keeps the conversation up to the restart, and removes the dead agent's files.

A Claude Code turn with file-backed stdio keeps running when the daemon is killed: the next daemon replays the handled log without repeating its writes, keeps the task In Progress, shows the output written before the restart once, restores the still unanswered question and never answers an answered request again, ignores a late reply to the old daemon's request and numbers its own requests past the old ones, delivers a steered follow-up, streams the rest of the turn to a watcher, records the turn's usage once, settles it through its outcome, and removes the finished run.

A Codex turn keeps running in its shared socket app-server when the daemon is killed: the next daemon reconnects to the same server (no second server, one connection per daemon), keeps the task In Progress with no restart notice, shows the output written before the restart exactly once, saves the question the server re-sends on resume and answers the re-sent approval exactly once, accepts a steered follow-up, streams the rest of the turn to a watcher, and settles it through the normal outcome path. A turn that finished while no daemon was connected settles from the server's state. A question the shared server raises on a thread no conversation owns gets no reply from the connected client, which leaves it for its owner instead of rejecting it.

A task starts with no recorded tokens, and its Token Stats modal says so plainly with no totals shown. Running a real Claude Code fixture turn parses that turn's reported usage into Playhouse's four buckets, adds them to the task's running totals, and records a per-turn row naming the provider and the tools, skills and MCP servers that ran in it. A second turn adds to the totals and appends its own row rather than replacing the first, and the per-tool rollup counts the turns each tool took part in. Call-level accounting spans the main agent and its subagents: an empty task's `callUsage` reports itself unavailable, and after a turn it reports exact model-call, total-sent, output and final-transcript figures read from the session files (counting each message ID once, ignoring repeated and zero-usage lines, and including the subagent's own file), which a second turn adds to rather than replaces. A Claude turn whose session files cannot be read still counts its calls live from the stream. The task card replaces its old dot with a compact live counter of total sent, which is hidden while that total is still zero, whose tooltip names the sent total, call count and final transcript size, and both the Token Stats context-menu item and a click on the counter itself, a button that highlights on hover, open a modal labelling 'Final transcript size' and 'Total sent (incl. subagents)' beside the call and output counts, the per-tool rollup and the per-turn breakdown. Excluding cache reads (uncached input + cache write + output, subagent included) is 855 per turn, doubling after a second turn, and also reaches the live stream when the session files cannot be read; an empty task reports it unavailable. A task saved before the cache split existed (call usage without the split, plus turn-level buckets) still loads, reports its call counts and total sent, omits the per-call excluding-cache figures, and falls back to the turn buckets minus cache reads (170 for 100 input, 50 output, 400 cache read and 20 cache write); its modal hides the Excluding cache reads headline. The modal also labels 'Excluding cache reads (incl. subagents)' with its main-agent and subagent split.

A Codex app-server fixture turn's usage reaches the same per-task totals and per-turn breakdown through Codex's own wire shape, mapping its cached-input bucket onto Playhouse's cache-read bucket and leaving cache-write at zero. The recorded turn row names Codex as its provider, Codex's input count includes its cached tokens, so the input bucket excludes them rather than counting them twice. Per-call usage notifications streamed before the turn ends, including those of a subagent thread that names its parent, reach the same call-level accounting once each (a repeated notification is ignored), and the Token Stats modal shows those Codex totals, call counts and final transcript size in the app. Excluding cache reads, the figure counts each call's uncached input plus cache write plus output, main thread and subagent alike (780), and the modal shows it with its main-agent and subagent split.

A task with no conversation reports its token map unavailable, with no wasters, tools or agents. After a Claude Code fixture turn whose session file logs every request (a shape, blobs, and transcript lines referenced by hash, including a parallel tool call sent as one message), the map reads the main agent and its subagent, and the main agent's final transcript tokens equal its last request's context exactly. The largest item is the MCP tool's 1,000-line log, ranked by the tokens it added, flagged as removed by the compaction, and sharing the tokens of the request it arrived in with its call by characters. The tools rollup ranks that MCP tool first by tokens added, the MCP server rollup counts its defined and called tools and what its definitions cost, the overhead lists the system prompt, each built-in tool definition and the server's definitions as sent with every request, the README read twice is one repeated result, the request that re-sent its context without the prompt cache is the one cache miss, and the compaction is counted. The Token Stats modal shows these in its Wasters, Tools & MCP and Overhead sections.

A Codex fixture turn whose thread and subagent have rollout files gives the same map from Codex's own format: a request was sent the instructions plus every item before its own output, the final transcript's tokens equal the last request's input exactly after a compaction replaced the history, Codex's unsaved tool definitions appear as one hidden-overhead item sent with every request, encrypted reasoning is shown by its size, the MCP tool's log is the largest item and was removed by the compaction, the repeated README read and the cache miss are reported, and the subagent's thread is its own agent. The raw input's final transcript lists the hidden overhead, the instructions and the replacement history once each without the removed log, and an item's full text, from a tool output or from the replacement history, reads back exactly as Codex saved it, in chunks, with its call named. The single-request scope rebuilds each Codex request from the rollout and labels it reconstructed: the latest request is the final transcript in order, request 4 flags both README reads and both of their outputs as exact duplicates, each request's items add up to the input Codex reported with its cached share as cache read and no cache write, and the JSON export holds the base instructions and the input items exactly as saved. The Token Stats modal shows the Codex wasters, the hidden overhead and the subagent, showing the log opens its full text, and the raw input's single request reads as reconstructed, with request 4's duplicates flagged.

A task with no conversation has no raw input: its page is empty and reading an item's text is not_found. After a Claude Code fixture turn, the raw input lists the final transcript with each item once across pages and without the log a compaction removed; the everything-sent scope adds what was removed, ordering by size lists the largest first, a search finds the log by a word only its full text contains, and a focus item reports its position. An item's full text reads back in chunks that end on a line break and join to the exact text, with the call that produced it named. An unknown agent or item is not_found, and an unknown order or a limit of zero is invalid_argument. In the app, View raw input opens the final transcript, scrolling loads the next page of rows, showing the largest waster opens it in the everything-sent scope with its full text, and scrolling that text reaches its last line.

After a Claude Code fixture session that resumes once its AGENTS.md changed, the raw input's single-request scope lists every item one request sent, in order and with nothing merged, and shows the latest request by default. A request after the resume carries both instruction copies in order, which differ and so are not flagged, while the date reminder sent twice word for word is flagged as a duplicate; a request before the resume carries one copy and no duplicates, and a search keeps each row's position. Each request reports Claude's input with its cache-read and cache-write split, and its items' sizes add up to that input. The request is labelled exact; its text export gives every item's full text under a header naming any duplicate, and its JSON export is the request body with the logged parameters, cache markers, system prompt, tools and messages verbatim, an earlier request's messages being a prefix of a later one's. A request number past the last is not_found, and zero or an unknown export format is invalid_argument. In the app, choosing Single request shows the latest request with its usage, both instruction copies unflagged and the repeated date reminder flagged, stepping back to a request before the resume shows one copy and no flags, Latest returns to the last request, and Copy all copies the whole request as JSON.

The token usage color maximum defaults to twenty million, round-trips through the CLI/XPC settings commands, and rejects a non-positive value as invalid_argument without changing the stored setting. The settings window shows the stored maximum and saves an edited one, and a task card's token counter re-colors when the maximum changes so the same usage reads hotter against a smaller ceiling.

A newly created Claude task reports cpu-usage as not running before any turn starts. While a real Claude Code fixture turn burns CPU in a real child process, two successive `task cpu-usage` reads establish a baseline and then a plausible non-zero percentage for the task's process tree, the task card's CPU bar reads cool green against the default multi-core ceiling and hot red once the ceiling is lowered to match that load, and the reading returns to not-running once the turn completes.

Two Codex tasks rooted in different repository folders share one real fixture app-server. Before any turn each reports cpu-usage as not running. While task A's turn runs a real CPU-burning child process in A's folder and task B's concurrent turn runs an idle child in B's folder, both children belong to the same app-server process; once a baseline is sampled, `task cpu-usage` attributes a plausible non-zero percentage to A and a near-zero one to B, and the task cards show A's CPU bar reading hot against a lowered ceiling beside B's visible but empty bar. Both readings return to not-running once the turns complete.

The CPU usage color maximum defaults to one fully busy core per logical CPU, round-trips through the CLI/XPC settings commands, and rejects a non-positive value as invalid_argument without changing the stored setting.

The Agents info section reads Claude and Codex plan usage and accounts through the bridge. A refresh reads both providers: Codex's account, plan, both rolling windows (5h and weekly) with percent used and reset times, and its credits balance come from the app-server, while Claude's usage is read with Claude Code's get_usage control request, which has none for this account yet, so Claude starts with a signed-in account and no usage. A Claude turn's rate_limit_event then fills Claude's 5h and weekly windows and its warning status from the stream, a usage watch already open receives that change as a pushed update without asking again, a fresh read returns the same values, and the last-known snapshot is persisted to disk. A later event whose window reset time has already passed reads back as reset (empty, no reset time) and lifts the limit status without any provider call. Because Claude Code streams rate_limit_event only when a limit's status changes, and a usage-based plan's event has no utilization, every finished Claude turn reads the plan's usage again through get_usage (skipping the local transcript scan) without a refresh: the read replaces the windows with the plan's current ones, keeps get_usage percents as percents, shows a usage-based plan's monthly extra usage as a Spend limit row with the reset time from the stream's overage event, and is persisted; a refresh reads it too, a reply without plan usage keeps the last known rows, a reached spend limit reads as the limit reached, and a usage request that is never answered times out, keeping the last known rows, so later reads work again. Switching the Codex account signs out, clears the cached usage, starts a new login that returns its sign-in URL, and shows the new account's account and usage after the login completes; switching the Claude account does the same through the CLI and drops the old account's usage. A signed-out provider reports loggedIn false with no account or usage, a login restores it, and an unknown provider is rejected as invalid_argument. In the visible UI the Agents info section sits at the bottom of the left sidebar, below the Scheduled Tasks button and inside it, titled Agents info, with a separate compact Claude block and Codex block, each showing its account and plan together on the row beneath the provider name, its window rows with percentages and reset times, and a switch-account button; Codex's credits show in its block and Claude's warning status shows as Near limit. After a Claude turn whose usage read reports the plan's spend, the open window shows Claude's Spend limit row with its percent and reset time and the updated 5h row without a relaunch. A signed-out provider shows a Log in button instead of usage, which starts the login and brings usage back, and switching the account signs out and in without asking when no task for that provider is running. The section is open by default and its title is a button that minimizes it: the agent blocks go away and the title moves down to rest at the bottom of the sidebar, and expanding brings them back; the choice is remembered, so a section minimized before a relaunch is still minimized afterwards. Every read reports whether each CLI is installed from the same executable lookup Playhouse launches it with; an agent whose CLI is not installed has no block, and with neither installed the section is not shown. While a task for a provider is running, its switch-account button first asks for confirmation naming how many of its tasks are running, and cancelling keeps the account.

When a standalone chat's agent loads an earlier page into its context with `chat page read`, the conversation renders one deterministic "Recalling <page title>" line per loaded page, titled from the page archive rather than from anything the agent wrote, in the order the pages were read. The lines are visible in the turn that read them without opening the Worked for disclosure, stay once the turn settles and after a later turn and a reopen, and the read commands really run and succeed so the history carries each call and the page's own title. The line is derived from Playhouse's own provider-neutral command activity (a shell call titled "Running <command>" for both Claude and Codex) and the page store, so provider selection cannot change it; one representative provider (Claude) covers the shared path.

The Skills page, opened from the composer's Skills button that replaced the paperclip, is a full page that slides in from the side over the task and fills the window, and its back button returns to the conversation. It lists the task's repository skills per repository (from each worktree's .agents/skills and .claude/skills, keyed by the source repository), the user's global skills (~/.agents/skills, Claude's skills folder, and Codex's legacy skills folder), and built-in skills (Codex's bundled .system skills, claude.ai-synced skills, and Claude Code's built-ins read from a provider session). Each user skill is shown as usable by both Claude and Codex; a skill linked into both layouts is one Linked entry, two different skills with the same name in one repository are flagged as a conflict, a SKILL.md without valid frontmatter is flagged invalid and usable by neither provider, a repository without skills shows an empty state, and built-ins name only the provider they ship with. Reading a skill returns its SKILL.md, and an unknown skill is not_found.

Creating a skill writes SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter into the open Agent Skills layout, ~/.agents/skills for a global skill or the chosen task worktree's .agents/skills for a repository skill; invalid names, a missing description, a duplicate name, and the built-in scope are rejected with nothing written. Editing saves the new SKILL.md exactly as written, keeping frontmatter Playhouse does not parse, and rejects a renamed or description-less frontmatter while keeping the file. Clicking a skill row opens the editor modal straight on its whole SKILL.md, frontmatter included, with no structured header form, and its Preview tab shows that Markdown rendered with the frontmatter as a table; saving there writes the edited file, a description-less edit is rejected in the editor while keeping the file, and after the editor closes the page still answers clicks. A structured CLI edit rewrites the header (reading a YAML list as one field), removes an emptied field, keeps frontmatter Playhouse does not edit, and rejects an unknown field or an empty description while keeping the file. Clicking a built-in skill with a folder opens it read-only, without Save. New Skill asks only for a name, a description, and instructions it can preview, and a header field given to the CLI's create is written into the new SKILL.md. Moving a skill between a repository and the global gallery moves its folder and rejects a move onto an existing name. Deleting removes the folder from disk, built-in skills are read-only, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the Skills page.

Turning a skill off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's settings, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the Skills page, and can be turned back on. The small switch flips as soon as it is clicked, and turning a skill on disk on or off never starts a Claude Code session. Making a skill available outside Playhouse writes a real symlink into the other provider's layout (an absolute link in Claude's global skills folder, a relative link inside the repository), after which the skill shows as Linked; an existing file at the link path is left untouched and the request fails with already_exists, removing the outside link deletes only the symlink and keeps the skill, and a skill without a link cannot be unlinked.

Pressing and holding a skill row starts selecting skills, with no separate Select button: each editable row shows a checkbox that a click toggles, built-in skills show none and cannot be selected, and the header shows how many are selected with Fix with Agent, Delete, and Done. Deleting the selection after one confirmation removes every selected skill folder, repository and global alike, from disk, leaves unselected skills in place, forgets a deleted skill's off state, and ends selecting. A batch that includes a read-only or unknown skill deletes nothing and fails with invalid_argument or not_found.

A conflicting or invalid skill offers Fix with Agent, and several selected skills can be fixed in one task. Fixing creates a task, on the source task's provider, whose saved prompt teaches the agent the skill format and lists each skill with its problem: repository skills by repository-relative path, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree of the source repository and committed and pushed like any code change, and global skills by absolute path, to be fixed in place with nothing to commit; the global skill folders are opened to the agent as context folders, and fixing only global skills needs no repository. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt as its own composer draft, leaving the composer empty and no unsent draft behind, so the turn runs in the new task's worktree with the global folders reachable. A skill with no problem, a built-in skill, an unknown skill, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn sees the skills Claude Code does not read natively: Playhouse passes a Playhouse-owned --add-dir wrapper whose .claude/skills links to the task worktree's and the global .agents/skills folders, leaves skills Claude already reads out of the wrapper, and turns disabled skills off for that run with --settings skillOverrides, without writing to the repository or Claude's settings. Using a skill from the Skills page puts /skill-name at the start of the composer and the message reaches Claude Code unchanged. The resumed second turn gets the same wrapper, and turning the skill back on drops the override.

A Codex turn sees the skills Codex does not read natively: Playhouse gives the shared app-server extra skill roots made of Playhouse-owned wrapper folders that link to the task worktree's and the global .claude/skills folders, leaves the cwd repository's .agents/skills to Codex, and starts the thread with a per-thread skills config that disables both the task's disabled skills and other tasks' bridged skills, without writing Codex's config.toml. Using a skill from the Skills page puts /skill-name in the composer, and the turn sends Codex a structured skill input naming that skill's SKILL.md alongside the text; a later turn without a skill sends none.

A repository skill created with Private on is written only to Playhouse's private skill store, in a folder keyed by the source repository and laid out as .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, with nothing written to the repository or the task worktree, whose git status stays clean. It is listed under its repository with scope private and a Private badge, every task on that repository sees it from its own worktree, and a task on another repository does not. A private skill cannot take a name that the committed skills of any of the task's repositories, the global skills, or the built-in skills already use, and a committed skill of the same name that appears later in a worktree takes precedence there: the private one is shown as Shadowed and used by neither provider. Editing saves the store's SKILL.md, a private skill cannot be linked outside Playhouse, Convert to Repository Skill moves it into the worktree's .agents/skills as a repository skill ready to commit, Make Private moves a repository skill back into the store and out of the worktree, Make Private to a repository moves a global skill into that repository's store, and Delete removes only its store folder.

A turn on a repository with private skills gets them as native skills, and a task on any other repository gets no extra folder, flag, or skill. Claude Code gets one more --add-dir, a Playhouse-owned wrapper named after the repository whose .claude/skills links to the store, so it lists the private skill and a /skill message reaches it unchanged; the link shows later edits, and a turned-off private skill is left out of the next turn without a skillOverrides entry and hidden from Codex threads. In a task with two repositories whose private skills share a name, each repository's wrapper is passed, and the later one is listed and invoked as /<repository>:<name>. Codex gets the repository's private wrapper among the shared app-server's extra skill roots, with other repositories' private skills disabled for its thread, and a /skill message, plain or namespaced, sends a structured skill input naming the private SKILL.md.

The Skills page, titled Skills, Rules & MCP, switches to its Rules list with a Skills | Rules | MCP picker. Rules lists each task repository's instruction files from its worktree (AGENTS.override.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and every .md file under .claude/rules, keyed by the source repository and the file's path), the user's global rules (~/.agents/AGENTS.md, Codex's AGENTS.md, and Claude's CLAUDE.md and rules folder), and the organization's managed CLAUDE.md. Each rule names the agents that follow it in Playhouse sessions and the ones that read it natively: a repository AGENTS.md beside a CLAUDE.md is followed by both but read natively only by Codex, ~/.agents/AGENTS.md is read natively by neither yet shared with both, a CLAUDE.md symlinked to AGENTS.md is one Linked rule read natively by both, AGENTS.override.md is Codex's own and leaves the AGENTS.md beside it to Claude, a .claude/rules file shows its paths globs, the managed CLAUDE.md is Claude's only and read-only, and an @import of a missing file is flagged as a problem. A repository without rules shows an empty state. Reading a rule returns its file exactly, and an unknown rule is not_found.

New Rule writes the shared AGENTS.md (the chosen task worktree's, or ~/.agents/AGENTS.md for a global rule) or, given a name, a topic file in .claude/rules (the worktree's, or Claude's global rules folder) whose paths frontmatter lists the globs given; empty instructions, an invalid name, globs without a name, the managed scope, and an existing file are rejected with nothing written, and the source checkout is left alone. Clicking a rule opens its editor on the whole file with a Markdown preview, and saving writes the file exactly as typed; empty instructions and a rules-folder file whose frontmatter never closes are rejected while keeping the file. The managed CLAUDE.md opens read-only without Save and can be neither edited nor deleted. Deleting a rule removes its file from disk, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the page.

A lone AGENTS.md that both CLIs already read on their own shows Both CLIs rather than Linked, since nothing links to it. Turning a rule off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's settings, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the page, and can be turned back on; the managed CLAUDE.md can't be turned off. A turned-off rule Codex reads itself, such as the working repository's AGENTS.md, still lists Codex and the page says Codex still reads it, while a rule only Playhouse shares, such as ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, reaches neither agent. Making ~/.agents/AGENTS.md available outside Playhouse writes absolute symlinks as Codex's AGENTS.md and Claude's CLAUDE.md, after which it is one Linked rule read natively by both; a repository CLAUDE.md gets a relative AGENTS.md symlink beside it. An existing file at a link path is left untouched and the request fails with already_exists without writing any link, a rule Codex has no place for can't be linked, and removing the outside link deletes only the symlinks.

A rule with a problem offers Fix with Agent, which creates a task on the source task's provider whose saved prompt explains how both agents read rules and lists each rule with its problem: repository rules by repository-relative path, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree and committed and pushed, and global rules by absolute path, to be fixed in place with their folder opened as a context folder, and fixing only global rules needs no repository. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt once and leaves no unsent draft. A rule with no problem, the managed rule, an unknown rule, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn follows the rules Claude Code does not read itself: after the task instructions, its appended system prompt carries ~/.agents/AGENTS.md with its @import of another file expanded inline, Codex's global AGENTS.md, and the AGENTS.md of the task's other repository, plus a pointer naming the globs and file of that repository's path-scoped rule; rules Claude reads itself, such as Claude's global CLAUDE.md and the working repository's CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, are not repeated. Because the working repository has both AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, --settings tells Claude Code to read both, and a rule turned off on the page is excluded for that run with claudeMdExcludes, without writing to the repository or Claude's settings. The resumed second turn carries the same rules, and turning the rule back on drops the exclusion.

A Codex turn follows the rules Codex does not read itself: after the task instructions, the thread starts with developer instructions carrying ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, Claude's global CLAUDE.md, and the working repository's CLAUDE.md and always-on .claude/rules files, with CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import left out because Codex already reads that file, and each path-scoped rule as a pointer naming its globs and file rather than its text. The working repository's AGENTS.md and Codex's global AGENTS.md are not repeated, a rule turned off on the page is left out, and Codex's config.toml is not written. A thread resumed on a fresh app-server gets the same rules.

The Skills page, titled Skills, Rules & MCP, switches to its MCP list with a Skills | Rules | MCP picker. MCP lists each task repository's servers from its worktree's .mcp.json and .codex/config.toml (keyed by the source repository and the server's name), the user's global servers from Claude Code's ~/.claude.json and Codex's config.toml, and the organization's managed-mcp.json. Each server shows its command or URL and only the names of its environment variables and headers, never their values, and names the agents that start it on their own and the ones Playhouse passes it to: a .mcp.json server is Claude's own and passed to Codex, a server defined the same way in both global files is one entry both CLIs start, a server only one CLI defines is passed to the other, an SSE server or one with a working folder reaches only the agent that can run it with the reason shown, a server Codex's config.toml turns off reaches neither, a server written inline in config.toml is listed but not editable, two global definitions that differ are flagged as a conflict, and the managed server is Claude's only and read-only. A repository without servers shows an empty state and an unreadable configuration file is reported. Reading a server returns its full definition, and an unknown server is not_found.

New Server writes a global server straight into both Claude Code's ~/.claude.json mcpServers and Codex's config.toml [mcp_servers] table, with ${NAME} environment references written as Codex env_vars and every other setting, comment and server in both files kept; a repository server goes into the chosen task worktree's .mcp.json and the source checkout is left alone. An invalid name, a missing command, an SSE server, a URL that is not http, an environment reference Codex can't pass through, the managed scope, and an existing name are rejected with nothing written. Clicking a server opens its editor, and saving rewrites it in every file that defines it while keeping each provider's own keys, such as Codex's startup_timeout_sec and Claude's oauth; an invalid edit and an edit to a server written inline in config.toml are rejected while keeping the files. Deleting a server removes it from every file that defines it, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the page. Right after a create closes its panel, one click on New Server opens it again.

Turning a server off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's configuration, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the page, and can be turned back on; the managed server can't be turned off. A turned-off server in Claude Code's own configuration still lists Claude and the page says Claude still starts it, so turning it off applies to Codex only, while a turned-off server only Codex defines reaches neither agent. Make Available Outside Playhouse writes a Claude-only global server into Codex's config.toml, a Codex-only one into Claude Code's ~/.claude.json, and a repository .mcp.json server into the worktree's .codex/config.toml, after which each is one entry both CLIs start; a conflicting server can't be linked and nothing is written.

A server whose definitions conflict offers Fix with Agent, which creates a task on the source task's provider whose saved prompt explains how both agents configure MCP servers and lists each server with its problem: repository servers by repository-relative file, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree and committed and pushed, and global servers by absolute file path, to be fixed in place with their folders opened as context folders. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt once and leaves no unsent draft. A server with no problem, a managed server, an unknown server, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn starts the servers Claude Code does not read itself: its --mcp-config carries Codex's own global servers (with env_vars passed as ${NAME}), the working repository's .codex/config.toml servers, and the other task repository's .mcp.json servers, but not the servers Claude Code already reads or ones turned off on the page. Its --settings starts the working repository's .mcp.json servers that are on with enabledMcpjsonServers and skips turned-off ones with disabledMcpjsonServers, without writing to the repository or either provider's configuration. The resumed second turn carries the same servers, and turning a server back on adds it.

A Codex turn starts the servers Codex does not read itself: the thread's mcp_servers config carries the working repository's .mcp.json servers and Claude Code's own global servers, translated so ${NAME} environment references become env_vars and an Authorization bearer token becomes bearer_token_env_var, leaves out an SSE server Codex can't run and the servers Codex already reads, and turns off a server Codex may read itself (from its config.toml or the working repository's .codex/config.toml) that is turned off on the page with enabled = false, without writing Codex's config.toml. Turning servers on or off on the page resumes the thread on its next turn with the new mcp_servers config.

Opening the MCP page asks both agents on its own, with no button to press, which servers they start and which need a sign-in, showing Checking sign-in… while they answer and asking again whenever the page is opened: Claude Code, asked with the task's own MCP bridge, reports each server including the ones Playhouse passes it, and Codex reports its own; a server that needs a sign-in shows a Sign in for Claude or Sign in for Codex badge on its row, and the claude.ai connectors and plugin servers Claude Code starts that no file defines are listed under Also started by Claude Code on the Managed tab, a connector that needs a sign-in with the same badge. Asking for one provider only asks that provider. An agent that can't be asked is reported by name on the page while the other agent's answer is still shown.

The Sign in for Claude or Sign in for Codex badge on a server is the button that signs in: it asks that agent to start the OAuth sign-in of that one server (Claude Code's mcp_authenticate, Codex's mcpServer/oauth/login) and returns the authorization link, which the page opens in the browser (a test build only records it, and never opens one) while the badge reads Waiting for sign-in…. A server both agents have shows one Sign in button per agent on the same row: each starts only its own agent's sign-in, waiting on one leaves the other clickable, and each badge clears on its own once that agent is signed in. The agent finishes the sign-in when the browser redirects back to it, and the page then checks again by itself and the badge goes away; waiting for it through the CLI keeps the bridge running and returns signed in. Starting one agent's sign-in never asks the other agent, a sign-in nobody finishes times out with a message that names the server, and waiting for a sign-in that was never started or was already reported with either agent, an unknown provider, and a blank server name are rejected or reported without starting anything.

The Plugins menu opens the Plugin Catalog, whose sidebar lists every atom (Stack, Text, Icon, Label, Button, Link, Spinner, Spacer, PillPicker, Card, Disclosure, Panel, Meter, Scroll, Divider, ChoiceBar, Toggle, TextField, Segmented, Menu, PressArea, Overlay, Editor, Popover, StepSlider) and the Task Item, Agents Info, Token Stats, Skills Page, Repository Chips and Composer examples; each atom page renders its JavaScript page through the React renderer into native SwiftUI with no plugin error and lists the atom's props. Clicking a Button atom runs its JavaScript onPress handler, whose state change commits a single text op on that Text's string node, and clicking a Disclosure's title runs its onToggle handler, which collapses it (its children hide while staying in the tree: one commit updating only the Disclosure's props and the state readout) and expands it again, and clicking a ChoiceBar's option runs its onChange handler with that option's value, which selects it (one commit updating only the ChoiceBar's props and the readout), while clicking the option already selected commits nothing, and the Scroll page's scroll view shrinks to its four rows, then, once added rows pass its 120-point maxHeight, stays 120 points tall and scrolls to reach the last row. On the Skills page's controls' pages, clicking the Toggle runs its onToggle handler, which flips it (one commit updating only the Toggle's props and the readout), typing in the TextField runs onChange with the new text, Return in it runs onSubmit and an arrow key runs onArrow with its direction, choosing a Segmented segment runs onChange with its value, choosing a Menu item runs onMenu with that item's id, and the PressArea tells a click (onPress) from a press and hold (onLongPress). On the Overlay page, the badge drawn over the chip's top trailing corner leaves the chip its own size and runs its own onPress. `plugin render` runs a plugin headlessly through the same runtime and node tree: the first render is one commit, each event sent by testID runs its handler and commits only the ops for the nodes that changed (a toggled label is one text op on one node), an interval advanced with --advance updates only its own node, and every bundled catalog page renders without errors. An unknown atom, an unknown or mistyped prop, a missing required prop, an event the atom doesn't raise, a child the atom can't hold, a string outside a Text, or a handler that throws is reported in errors with exit 1 (a mistyped or missing prop, decoded straight from the plugin's values, names its path and what is wrong, such as size: expected a number, found a string or options.0.label: missing), and an event for a missing testID, an event the atom has no handler for, or an unknown catalog page is refused as invalid_argument. Commits, the plugin's props and event values cross between JavaScript and Swift as JavaScript values with JSON.stringify's rules: props keep their types and nesting, NaN becomes null, a Date becomes its ISO string, undefined, function and inherited fields are left out of nested values, toJSON is called once per value (one that returns itself gives an empty object), an event value arrives as a string, and a circular prop or an op whose node id is out of range is reported in errors. The Button page also shows a link-style Button and a large one (taller than a regular Button), each running onPress, the Menu page's disabled Run Now item is shown but can't be chosen, and the Icon page draws the app logo asset in its own colors (original) in a 50-point frame with its accessibility label; a mistyped original or Menu item disabled is reported with its path.

The Plugin Catalog's Stack page draws a surface on a Stack in both axes, while its Stacks without surface props draw nothing: a column filled accent at 0.18 with an accent border and an 8-point radius keeps its children at its top leading corner, inside its padding, when its 220-point minWidth and 90-point minHeight are larger than they are; a capsule row filled #2E7D32 with a dashed border lays its icon and text out side by side on that green; and a border-only Stack with align unset (a Stack's default, center) and fillWidth stretches across the page, draws its border and no fill with rounded corners, and keeps its text centered both ways in its 60-point minHeight. The Panel page shows each Panel beside the Stack it is shorthand for (a column Stack with group, fill primary at 0.05 and radius 8 unless set), and each pair is the same size, including the accent Log in Panel and the single decorated row Stack that replaces its nested row. `plugin render` reports the surface props on those nodes with no errors and none on the plain Stacks, and a mistyped surface prop on a Stack (fill, fillOpacity, cornerRadius, capsule, strokeWidth or dash) or an unknown one (shadow, or axis on a Panel) is reported in errors with exit 1, naming the prop and what is wrong. The ChoiceBar page also composes the bar from atoms, a decorated row Stack of Buttons each marked selected (the Button's selected prop) around a decorated Stack with a Text: it is the same size as the ChoiceBar atom beside it, its Overview button carries the selected trait, and clicking Wasters runs its onPress, which moves the selected trait to it (Composed: wasters) while the ChoiceBar atom stays on Overview; a mistyped selected on a Button is reported with its path.

The Plugin Catalog's Task Item page shows the task item composed in JavaScript from atoms beside the native SwiftUI task item built from the same atoms and sample data: both show the same title, progress report, status message, token counter, conflicts button, pull-request mode pill and pull-request link with the same sizes, and the JavaScript tree uses only atoms with the native card's identifiers and context menu. Blocking the JavaScript item changes only its status message and the toggle's label (one commit: text, update, text on three nodes) while the native item keeps its own state, clicking the JavaScript card runs its onPress handler (Opened 1 times, one text op), choosing Merge in its mode pill runs onChange (Last: mode merge) without re-rendering the title or the card, and right-clicking the JavaScript card offers the native card's menu, whose Move to Done runs onMenu with its id (Last: menu done). The time row is one flat row: the clock, the created time and the token counter are siblings in one stack, so the time shows in full (Nov 8, 2026), as wide in the JavaScript item as in the native one and left of the counter.

A task whose conversation hasn't started is scheduled once (the composer's schedule hint, or schedule set --once); scheduling saves the prompt as the schedule's own payload without starting a turn, keeps the task in Backlog with a clock badge, and lists it in schedule list. Removing the schedule in the hint before Send turns the clock button off and returns Send to sending. A time in the past or a blank prompt is rejected with invalid_argument. A tick before the time does nothing; a tick 30 minutes after it, inside the one-hour grace period, sends the scheduled prompt to the provider, clears the schedule, and the task follows the ordinary board lifecycle. A second tick doesn't run it again, and a task that has started can't be scheduled. The app bundle carries the scheduler LaunchAgent (<bundle-id>.scheduler.plist running playhouse-cli schedule tick every 60 seconds), and a plain tick on the real clock fires a schedule that has come due.

A scheduled run more than one hour late is not started. A one-time task lands in Blocked with a 'Missed scheduled run' message and its prompt kept as an unsent draft, and sending that draft starts it. A recurring schedule ticked a week late creates exactly one Blocked run task linked to its schedule, skips the older missed occurrences, and moves its next run into the future. A due run whose provider can't start lands in Blocked saying the scheduled run couldn't start, with its prompt kept as the draft.

A recurring schedule needs a title, and a weekday when it repeats weekly; once confirmed, its template is absent from the board and task list but listed by schedule list and on the Scheduled Tasks page. A due tick creates a new board task with the schedule's title and context folders, linked by scheduleSourceTaskID, sends the prompt, records the run on the template and advances its next run by one day. A paused schedule doesn't fire, Run now starts a run immediately, and clearing the schedule turns the template into an ordinary Backlog task.

The Scheduled Tasks sidebar button opens the Scheduled Tasks page, whose New Task (header, or the button on the empty page) opens a task conversation with the schedule hint already open on Recurring. Opening a scheduled task shows its confirmed prompt with the schedule button on and Send in schedule mode, and its hint shows the saved repeat, day and time; changing its title and repeat in the hint and confirming with Send persists across fresh CLI reads, keeps the time, and starts no turn. Deleting a schedule removes it from schedule list and from the page. Sending a one-time scheduled task by hand ends its schedule, so a later tick sends nothing more; a recurring template rejects a send with invalid_transition; and clearing a schedule keeps its prompt as the task's draft.
